{{Short description|American distance runner}}
'''Erica Larson Baron''' (born August 11, 1971) is a [[chemist]] at the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]] and a champion [[fell running|mountain runner]]. She has won the [[Pikes Peak]] [[marathon]] on five occasions, more than any other woman since the event's inception in 1959.<ref name="nowhere">[https://www.skyrunner.com/story/2005p13.htm "Out of nowhere: Marathon’s winningest woman is an unlikely hill climber"], Meri-Jo Borzilleri, ''[[The Gazette (Colorado Springs)|The Gazette]]'', August 14, 2005</ref><ref name="profile">[http://www.usatf.org/athletes/bios/MountainUltraTrail/Larson_Erica.asp Erica Larson biography], USATF website</ref><ref name="pp_winners">[http://www.skyrunner.com/ppresults/ppwinners.htm List of Pikes Peak marathon winners] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071017214048/http://skyrunner.com/ppresults/ppwinners.htm |date=2007-10-17 }}, [[Matt Carpenter (runner)|Matt Carpenter]], Skyrunner.com</ref>

She was raised in [[Fond du Lac, Wisconsin]], the daughter of two [[music teacher]]s, before enrolling at [[Marquette University]] in [[Milwaukee, Wisconsin]]. After graduating with a [[Bachelor's degree]] in [[chemistry]], she earned her [[doctorate]] at the [[University of Kansas]] aged 27, before moving to [[Los Alamos, New Mexico]]. The city, at over 7,001&nbsp;ft above [[sea level]], offers an extensive network of nearby trails which Larson frequents while training.<ref name="nowhere"/> On August 28, 2005, she married fellow scientist and runner Miles Baron, who won the [[Bandelier]] marathon in [[New Mexico]] for three straight years until the race was cancelled in 2005.<ref name="nowhere"/>

After participating in the Pikes Peak ascent in 1994 and 1998, Larson won the "up and down" marathon at her first attempt in 1999, and repeated this result in each of the following three years. She was runner-up to [[Angela Mudge]] in 2003, but regained the top step on the podium with her fifth win overall in 2004, when the [[Scotland|Scottish]] runner did not return to defend her title. Her preparations for the 50th-anniversary marathon in 2005 were curtailed by a [[calf muscle]] injury and [[strep throat]], but she reversed her earlier decision to withdraw, saying "I'd be really bummed out if I didn't run it this year". Despite her health issues she still managed to finish third.<ref name="sky_db">[http://www.skyrunner.com/search/find.asp?Last=LARSON&Mi=J&First=ERICA Pikes Peak race results for Erica Larson], Skyrunner.com</ref><ref name="find">{{cite news |last=Borzilleri |first=Meri-Jo |title=Larson changes her mind, decides to race after all |date=August 14, 2005 |work=[[The Gazette (Colorado Springs)|The Gazette]] |via=[[FindArticles]] |url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4191/is_20050814/ai_n14881774/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110616054241/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_qn4191/is_20050814/ai_n14881774/ |archive-date=June 16, 2011 |url-status=usurped}}</ref>

She is also a two-time winner of the [[Leadville]] Marathon, and finished 34th at the U.S. Women's Olympic Marathon Trials in 2004, which she describes as her proudest achievement.<ref name="nowhere"/><ref name="profile"/>
